content_voiceover: Now we bring thrombin, labeled here as two a, into the picture. Thrombin is a serine protease, and its job at this step is highly specific proteolysis, it cleaves the fibrinopeptide A and fibrinopeptide B caps right off the amino termini in the central E domain. You can see the arrow showing those small FPA and FPB fragments being released and floating away once thrombin acts. Removing those peptides does two important things, it unmasks polymerization sites on the E domain, and it exposes new positively charged ends that can dock into complementary pockets on the D domains of neighboring fibrinogen molecules. This is the essential proteolytic step that converts fibrinogen into fibrin monomer, and it's the rate limiting chemical event that allows soluble fibrinogen to start assembling into an insoluble mesh. Everything downstream, from monomer to polymer to a stable cross-linked clot, depends on this single cleavage event.
keypoints: Thrombin, factor IIa, is a serine protease acting on fibrinogen
Thrombin cleaves off fibrinopeptide A and fibrinopeptide B from the E domain
Cleavage unmasks new polymerization sites on the E domain
Exposed sites bind complementary pockets on D domains of other molecules
This proteolytic step converts fibrinogen into fibrin monomer
keypoint_voiceover: Thrombin acts as a serine protease here, snipping fibrinopeptides A and B off the E domain of fibrinogen. That cleavage unmasks binding sites that dock into D domains on neighboring molecules, converting fibrinogen into fibrin monomer, the essential first step toward clot formation.
